summaries.example: Imagine a soft lump of clay. On Monday, it is just a lump. On Tuesday, an artist shapes it into a person-shaped statue. Is there one thing that changed shape, or are there two things in the same place: the statue and the lump? The statue could be ruined by squashing, while the clay could still exist as a lump. This makes the question tricky.
summaries.summary: Material constitution is about how physical stuff relates to the objects made from it. A lump of clay can be shaped into a statue, but the clay and statue seem to have different features: the clay existed before the statue, and the clay might survive being squashed while the statue would not. Philosophers use this puzzle, along with stories about changing ships and objects losing parts, to ask what makes something the same thing over time. One answer says the statue and clay are distinct objects in the same place. Other answers use time-parts, deny that some ordinary objects exist, say an object’s most important kind controls its identity, reject absolute sameness, or say the dispute may depend on how words are used.
key_ideas: A statue and the clay used to make it seem alike, but they may have different histories and abilities to change.
The Ship of Theseus asks whether a ship stays the same after all its boards are replaced.
Some philosophers say the statue and clay are two objects that share one place.
Other philosophers deny that some objects exist, say objects have time-parts, or think the disagreement is partly about language.
summaries.why_it_matters: The puzzle helps us examine everyday ideas about objects, change, and sameness. It also shows that simple questions such as “Is this the same thing?” can have several reasonable answers once we consider shape, matter, parts, time, and language.

important_terms.definition: The relationship between material stuff and an object made from that stuff, such as clay and a statue.
Being exactly the same thing, not merely being in the same place or made of the same material.
An object made of parts, such as a ship made of boards or a statue made of clay.
An object that lasts through time, even though it may change in shape or parts.

questions_to_think_about: If every board of a toy boat is replaced, is it still the same boat?
Can two objects be in exactly the same place at once?
Could a statue exist before anyone shaped the clay?
Which matters more for being the same object: the material, the shape, or the history?

summaries.example: A sculptor buys a lump of clay on Monday and calls it Lump. On Tuesday, she forms it into a statue called David. If David is not present on Monday but Lump is, Leibniz’s Law suggests that David and Lump are not identical, because identical things must share their properties. Yet ordinary speech invites us to say that David is simply the clay shaped as a statue. The case therefore creates pressure either to accept coincident objects or to revise one of the assumptions behind the argument.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates puzzles about the relation between matter and the objects made from it. The statue-and-clay case is especially important: the clay exists before the statue, while the statue and clay appear to have different persistence conditions. If these claims are accepted, the statue is not identical to the clay, apparently requiring distinct objects to coincide. The constitution view accepts this result but faces questions about how coincident duplicates differ and why there are not arbitrarily many coincident objects. Temporal-parts theorists model persistence as extension through time, while eliminativists reject some composite objects. Other strategies appeal to dominant kinds, relative identity, or deflationism, which treats the dispute as potentially rooted in competing uses of existence and object-language. The entry also connects these issues to the Ship of Theseus, loss and addition of parts, and ordinary judgments about objects.
key_ideas: The central statue-and-clay argument contrasts differences in history and persistence with the intuition that one piece of matter is simply shaped into a statue.
The constitution view accepts distinct objects that coincide, but must explain why apparently identical objects differ in kind and persistence conditions.
Four-dimensionalism explains persistence through temporal parts and avoids some coincidence worries, though difficult cases remain when objects share all their temporal parts.
Eliminativist theories avoid the puzzle by denying statues, lumps, or other composites, but then must explain ordinary talk and the nature of basic parts.
The dominant-kinds view and relative identity revise how kinds or identity work; deflationism instead questions whether the dispute is a genuine disagreement about reality.
The classic puzzles include the Debtor’s Paradox, Dion and Theon, the Ship of Theseus, and the statue-and-clay case.
summaries.why_it_matters: Material constitution tests basic assumptions about identity, existence, parts, and change. The debate matters because our ordinary categories—statue, lump, ship, person—seem useful but may not line up neatly with one metaphysical account. Studying the competing replies also illustrates how philosophers respond to a puzzle: by accepting surprising entities, revising persistence, denying objects, changing logic or semantics, or challenging the problem’s framing.

important_terms.definition: The metaphysical relation between material matter and an object constituted by it; the constitution view treats the objects as distinct rather than identical.
Numerical sameness: x and y are one and the same object, not merely similar or made of the same parts.
Leibniz’s principle that identical objects must have all the same properties.
The thesis that two distinct objects can occupy the same place at the same time, often while sharing material parts.
The view that objects persist by having different parts at different times, analogous to having different spatial parts in different places.
A view that denies the existence of some composite objects, ranging from the denial of all composites to more limited proposals.
The proposal that an object’s dominant kind determines its persistence conditions when it belongs to more than one kind.
The view that sameness is always sameness of a particular kind, such as being the same statue, rather than absolute identity.

questions_to_think_about: Does sharing all the same material parts force two things to be identical? Why or why not?
Can a theory explain why a lump survives squashing while a statue does not without merely restating their different names?
Would a world with only simples—objects without proper parts—fit our ordinary descriptions of statues and people?
If sameness is always relative to a kind, can “the same ship” fail to be transitive?
When is a philosophical disagreement genuinely verbal rather than a disagreement about what exists?

summaries.example: Suppose your school replaces the parts of a bicycle one at a time. After several years, none of the original pieces remain. Is it still your bicycle? Now suppose someone saves the old pieces and rebuilds a bicycle from them. Which bicycle, if either, is the original? The Ship of Theseus gives this problem a famous form. It shows that “same object” might depend on how we track parts, shape, history, or use.
summaries.summary: Material constitution asks how an object relates to the material that makes it. A lump of clay exists before it is shaped into a statue, and the clay may survive being squashed even though the statue would not. This suggests that the statue and clay are different, but our ordinary way of speaking suggests that the statue is just the clay in a new form. Related puzzles ask whether a person survives losing a foot, whether a ship survives replacement of every plank, and whether a rebuilt ship is the original. Philosophers respond in several ways. Some accept distinct objects in one place, some give objects temporal parts, and some deny that certain composite objects exist. Other proposals say that one kind is more important than another, that identity is always relative to a kind, or that the disagreement is partly about language.
key_ideas: The same object can seem to depend on different rules: keeping its material, keeping its shape, or keeping a continuous history.
The statue-and-clay puzzle asks whether one thing can be both a statue and a lump, or whether there are two objects sharing one location.
The constitution view says the statue and clay are distinct but related; critics ask what explains their differences.
Temporal-parts theory compares persistence through time with having parts spread through space.
Eliminativists avoid some puzzles by denying that certain ordinary composites exist, while other theories revise kinds or identity.
Deflationism suggests that some disputes may concern meanings of words such as “object” or “exists,” although applying this idea is difficult.
summaries.why_it_matters: These puzzles make us question ideas we usually take for granted: what counts as an object, how change affects identity, and whether matter alone determines what something is. They also show why philosophers compare several explanations instead of quickly choosing the answer that first feels natural.

important_terms.definition: The connection between the material a thing is made from and the thing itself, such as a lump of clay and a statue.
Being one and the same object, rather than merely looking alike or occupying the same location.
An object built from smaller parts, such as a ship built from planks.
The ability of an object to continue existing through change.
The view that two different objects can occupy one location at the same time, often because one constitutes the other.
The view that an object has different parts at different times, as a road has different sections in different places.
A theory that removes some puzzling objects from its account of what exists.
A kind that determines how an object can continue to exist when it also belongs to another kind.

questions_to_think_about: Which bicycle would you call the original in the example, and what rule are you using?
Could two objects share all their physical parts but still have different possibilities?
Does a thing begin to exist when its matter is gathered, when it is shaped, or when it receives a function?
Would it be easier to solve these puzzles by saying that some ordinary objects do not really exist?
Can changing the meaning of a word solve a disagreement, or might it only hide the disagreement?
